To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) technologies licensed to foreign firms or spin-offs are less likely to be commercialized, (ii) technologies licensed to firms are more likely to be commercial, (iii) collaborative inventions are more likely to commercialized, (iv) inventions by senior scientists are more likely to licensed, but less likely to commercialized.
the licensing of technologies to foreign firms and the commercialization of technologies licensed by spin-offs are negatively correlated.

i) information asymmetry and knowledge transfer between public research organizations and firms are key determinants of technology licensing and successful commercializations; ii) foreign licensees and spin-offs are more important for technology licensing than for commercialization of inventions, while collaborative inventions have the opposite characteristics; iii) senior scientists are more likely to license their inventions but less likely to have them successfully commercialized; iv) the key role of spin-offs for technology licensing from a public research organization is particularly important for senior scientists.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of knowledge transfer and information asymmetry in the commercialization of inventions by a public research organization.
the role of public research organizations in technology transfer and commercialization.
the effects of imperfect knowledge transfer on technology licensing and commercialization.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the transfer of technology from public research is not as easy as one might have expected.
knowledge transfer is imperfect and that information asymmetry is a major factor in explaining the licensing and commercialization success of public research.
the more complex the knowledge transfer process becomes, the less likely it is that a technology is commercialized.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the transfer of knowledge from public research organizations is a complex process, in which information asymmetry, imperfect knowledge transfer, and other factors play a crucial role.
knowledge transfer is imperfect, especially for inventions made by senior scientists.
the licensing of a technology is an important, but insufficient, step in the commercialization process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the licensing and successful exploitation of public research inventions is not a simple matter of technology transfer.
public research organizations should be aware of the importance of knowledge transfer to commercial partners and should take steps to improve it.
the success of knowledge transfer from public research depends not only on the characteristics of the invention but also on the type of organization that licenses it.
